Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 59
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Professor
  trauma_type: Trauma to a loved one
  pcl5: 54

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Visual (Water/Flooding): Water, flooding, or large bodies of water, Olfactory (Smell): Related smells, Stress: Stress
  Threat: Body Reacts Before Mind: My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think, Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame, Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place

Vignette:
Kwame Mensah, a 59-year-old African American professor who had built his life around structure, reading, and long stretches of quiet work, came to treatment after several months of feeling as though his body no longer belonged to him in the ordinary spaces of his day. The event that changed things had involved someone he loved dearly: years earlier, while visiting family near a large lake, his younger brother had been swept into dangerous water after an unexpected flooding surge. Kwame had been present in the chaos that followed, and although he tried to focus on what could be done, the memory that stayed with him was not a clear sequence of events so much as the force of the scene itself — the rushing water, the panic in the air, the overwhelming sense of helplessness as the situation unfolded around him. In the weeks afterward he found that certain details would return with particular sharpness, especially when he encountered water that looked too still and deep or too wide to trust. Even the smell of dampness after rain, a musty odor in an older building, or the scent that rose from wet earth on a humid day could make him go rigid before he understood why.

Kwame had first noticed the change in modest ways. On walks across campus he began choosing routes that kept him away from fountains, drainage channels, and the reflecting pool outside the library. When he was assigned to teach in a seminar room on the ground floor after heavy rain, he found himself glancing repeatedly toward the windows and the hallway, unsettled by the sight of water streaming down the curb outside. He told himself he was being sensible, yet the reaction in his body often arrived before any deliberate thought. His heart would startle, his muscles would tighten, and for a moment he would have the unsettling impression that danger was already present, even if he was standing in a dry classroom or sitting alone in his office. What distressed him most was that he knew, rationally, that he was in safe surroundings, and still he could not settle. In his apartment at night, even with the doors locked and the room quiet, he would lie awake feeling keyed up and unable to relax, as if his body were continuing to listen for something that had already happened years before.

Over time, he became more careful about what he exposed himself to. He stopped taking the scenic route by the river after work and declined invitations that involved boating, lakeside events, or outdoor gatherings near large bodies of water. When a colleague suggested a weekend retreat at a hotel with water views, Kwame declined with an excuse about grading. He also became increasingly attentive to smells that others would barely notice. If rain had left the air heavy and earthy, or if he passed a place where water and mildew mixed, he would feel a sudden tightening in his chest and an immediate urge to leave. At the university, this made ordinary workdays more difficult than he wanted to admit. As a professor, he spent much of his day in buildings with old plumbing, wet umbrellas near the entrance during storms, and the stress of deadlines, student meetings, and administrative demands. On high-pressure days he noticed the symptoms more vividly: after a difficult departmental meeting, his body seemed to react as if to threat, leaving him agitated and on guard long after the meeting ended. He had become aware that stress itself could make everything feel closer, sharper, and harder to dismiss.

Kwame was not a man given to dramatics, and he was uncomfortable naming what he felt, yet he could not deny the persistence of strong negative emotions that surfaced around the reminders. Fear came first, then sometimes horror at the memory of what had happened to his brother, and at moments a wave of guilt for not having been able to prevent it. There were times he also felt shame for how unsettled he had become, as if someone with his age, education, and position should have been able to contain himself better. He kept these reactions largely private. As a single man accustomed to managing his own life, he had become more self-contained, spending more evenings alone and avoiding situations where he might be caught off guard by water-related reminders. Yet the cost of that caution was increasingly visible. He was less spontaneous, less willing to linger outdoors after rain, and more exhausted from the effort of staying composed. His colleagues saw only that he had become quieter and more exacting in his scheduling; they did not see how much energy it took for him to move through days that might unexpectedly include flooding imagery, damp smells, or the pressure of stress.

He finally sought help when he recognized that his efforts to stay in control were no longer enough to make him feel settled. What brought him in was not a single dramatic episode, but the accumulation of nights when he could not relax and days when his body reacted before his mind had caught up. He described wanting to understand why ordinary reminders could still make him feel as though something terrible were about to happen. More than anything, Kwame hoped to regain a sense of ease in places that were objectively safe and to stop feeling as though he had to organize his life around the possibility that water, a smell, or a stressful moment might suddenly carry him back to that flooding scene and his brother’s peril.
